'''''Agonis flexuosa''''', commonly known as '''peppermint''',<ref name=FB>{{FloraBase | name = ''Agonis flexuosa'' | id = 5316}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Myrtaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to the [[Southwest Australia|southwest of Western Australia]].  The [[Noongar]] peoples know the tree as '''wanil''', '''wonnow''', '''wonong'''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kippleonline.net/bobhoward/plantsframe.html|title=Noongar names for plants|access-date=24 November 2016|publisher=kippleonline.net|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161120071826/http://www.kippleonline.net/bobhoward/plantsframe.html|archive-date=2016-11-20|url-status=dead}}</ref> or '''wannang'''.<ref name=green>{{cite web|url=http://www.greenskills.org.au/pub/pamph/plants.html|title=Plants of the Denmark walk trails: Traditional Noongar Names and Uses|access-date=29 May 2017|publisher=Green skills Inc.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170712131022/http://www.greenskills.org.au/pub/pamph/plants.html|archive-date=12 July 2017|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref> It is a tree or shrub with pendulous, very narrowly elliptic, narrowly elliptic or narrowly egg-shaped leaves, white flowers with 20 to 25 [[stamen]]s opposite the [[sepal]]s and broadly top-shaped to broadly cup-shaped [[Capsule (fruit)|capsules]]. 

== Description ==
''Agonis flexuosa'' is usually a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|10|m}}, sometimes a wind-swept [[Mallee (habit)|mallee]] or almost prostrate shrub. Its branchlets are often twisted or zig-zagged, and usually [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]] as they age. The leaves are very narrowly elliptic, narrowly elliptic or narrowly egg-shaped, {{cvt|80–135|mm}} long and {{cvt|3.5–12|mm}} wide and [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] or on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] up to {{cvt|5|mm}} long. The leaves sometimes have soft, silky hairs when young, but become glabrous as they age, and have a prominent mid-vein and usually two other veins. The flowers are arranged in clusters {{cvt|10–15|mm}} wide with broadly egg-shaped [[bract]]s and elliptic [[bracteole]]s {{cvt|1–2|mm}} long. The [[Hypanthium|floral tube]] is {{cvt|1.5–2|mm}} long and the [[sepal]]s are {{cvt|1–2|mm}} long with silky, greyish hairs. The petals are white, spatula-shaped, {{cvt|3–6|mm}} long and there are 20 to 25 stamens with 3 to 5, sometimes up to 7 opposite the sepals, but none opposite the petals. The [[Stamen#filament|filaments]] are {{cvt|1–1.5|mm}} long and the [[Style (botany)|style]] {{cvt|1–2.5|mm}} long. Flowering occurs from July to December, and the capsule is broadly top-shaped to broadly cup-shaped, {{cvt|2.5–4|mm}} long, in clusters {{cvt|6–10|mm}} wide.<ref name="FB" /><ref name="Nuytsia">{{cite journal |last1=Wheeler |first1=Judith R. |last2=Marchant |first2=Neville G. |title=A revision of the Western Australian genus ''Agonis'' (Myrtaceae) and two new segregate genera ''Taxandria'' and ''Paragonis''. |journal=Nuytsia |date=2007 |volume=16 |issue=2 |pages=400–403 |doi=10.58828/nuy00414 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/313227#page/142/mode/1up |access-date=5 August 2024}}</ref><ref name = "Rippey">{{cite book |last1= Rippey|first1=Elizabeth |last2=Rowland (Reinette) |first2=Barbara |title=Coastal plants: Perth and the south-west region |orig-year=1995 |edition= 2nd |year=2004 |publisher= [[University of Western Australia|UWA]] Press |location= Perth |isbn= 1-920694-05-6|pages= 41}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
This species was first formally described in 1809 by [[Carl Ludwig Willdenow]] who gave it the name ''Metrosideros flexuosa'' in his ''Enumeratio Plantarum Horti Regii Botanici Berolinensis''.<ref name="apni3">{{cite web |title=''Metrosideros flexuosa'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/542256|publisher=Australian Plant Name Index |access-date=5 August 2024}}</ref><ref name="Willd.">{{cite book |last1=Willdenow |first1=Carl Ludwig |title=Enumeratio Plantarum Horti Regii Botanici Berolinensis |volume=1 |date=1809 |page=514 |url=https://archive.org/details/dclwilldenowenum00will/page/513/mode/1up |access-date=6 August 2024}}</ref> In 1830, [[Robert Sweet (botanist)|Robert Sweet]] transferred the species to ''Agonis'' in his ''Hortus Britannicus''.<ref name="apni2">{{cite web |title=''Agonis flexuosa'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/492676|publisher=Australian Plant Name Index |access-date=5 August 2024}}</ref><ref name="Sw.">{{cite book |last1=Sweet |first1=Robert |title=Hortus Britannicus |date=1830 |publisher=James Ridgway |location=London |page=209 |edition=2nd |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/45630940#page/233/mode/1up |access-date=5 August 2024}}</ref>

The genus name ''Agonis'' comes from the Greek ''agon'' meaning 'a gathering' or 'collection', probably referring to the flower heads<ref name="ASG1">{{cite book |last1=George |first1=Alex |last2=Sharr |first2=Francis |title=Western Australian Plant Names and Their Meanings |date=2021 |publisher=Four Gables Press |location=Kardinya, WA |isbn=9780958034180 |page=129 |edition=4th}}</ref> and the [[specific epithet]] (''flexuosa'') is [[Latin]] for 'zig-zag', referring to the zig-zag branches.<ref name="ASG2">{{cite book |last1=George |first1=Alex |last2=Sharr |first2=Francis |title=Western Australian Plant Names and Their Meanings |date=2021 |publisher=Four Gables Press |location=Kardinya, WA |isbn=9780958034180 |page=200 |edition=4th}}</ref>

In 1844, [[Johannes Conrad Schauer]] describes two varieties of ''A. flexuosa'' and the names are accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]]:
* ''Agonis flexuosa'' var. ''flexuosa''<ref name="APC1">{{cite web |title=''Agonis flexuosa'' var. ''flexuosa'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/78178 |publisher=Australian Plant Census |access-date=5 August 2024}}</ref> is a tree up to {{cvt|10|m}} high or a wind-pruned shrub, the branches sometimes zig-zagged, with leaves very narrowly elliptic, narrowly elliptic or narrowly egg-shaped, {{cvt|80–135|mm}} long and more or less flat and not twisted or wavy, and only the mid-vein prominent, the petals {{cvt|3–6|mm}} long, usually 4 or 5 stamens opposite each petal, and the capsules usually {{cvt|2.5–3.5|mm}} wide. This variety mostly flowers from September to December.<ref name="Nuytsia" />
* ''Agonis flexuosa '' var. ''latifolia''<ref name="APC2">{{cite web |title=''Agonis flexuosa'' var. ''latifolia'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/78184 |publisher=Australian Plant Census |access-date=5 August 2024}}</ref> (previously known as ''Billotia flexuosa'' var. ''latifolia'' <small>[[Christoph Friedrich Otto|Otto]] & [[A.Dietr.]]</small>)<ref name="apni">{{cite web |title=''Billotia flexuosa'' var. ''latifolia'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/662088|publisher=Australian Plant Name Index |access-date=5 August 2024}}</ref> is a shrub or small tree tup to {{cvt|4|m}} high, the branches commonly zig-zagged, with leaves usually narrowly egg-shaped, {{cvt|18–45|mm}} long and often twisted, the mid-vein and two longitudinal veins prominent, the petals {{cvt|3–4|mm}} long, with 3 or 4 stamens opposite each petal, and the capsules {{cvt|3–4|mm}} wide. This variety mainly flowers from September to November.<ref name="Nuytsia" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Agonis flexuosa'' var. ''flexuosa'' occurs in a range of habitats from coastal heath to woodland or forest and in a range of soils, in the [[Esperance Plains]], [[Geraldton Sandplains]], [[Jarrah Forest]], [[Swan Coastal Plain]] and [[Warren bioregion|Warren]] bioregions of south-western Western Australia,<ref name="Nuytsia" /><ref name="FB1">{{FloraBase | name = ''Agonis flexuosa'' var. ''flexuosa'' | id = 17202}}</ref> and var. ''latifolia'' mainly grows in sandy soil in heath, shrubland or woodland between [[Walpole, Western Australia|Walpole]] and [[Cheyne Beach Whaling Station|Cheyne Beach]] in the Esperance Plains, Jarrah Forest and Warren bioregions, with a record from the [[Stirling Range]].<ref name="Nuytsia" /><ref name="FB2">{{FloraBase | name = ''Agonis flexuosa'' var. ''latifolia'' | id = 17203}}</ref>

==Uses==
===Use in horticulture===
Horticultural variants are probably derived from the widespread population, growing as shrubs or trees and perhaps being flowerless. Some commercially produced cultivars include ''Agonis'' ‘Belbra Gold’ and ''Agonis'' ‘Fairy Foliage’.<ref name="Nuytsia" />

===Aboriginal use===
The [[Noongar]] peoples used the plant leaves as an [[antiseptic]]; sapling trunks were used as spear shafts and digging sticks.<ref name=green/>
